To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of PTSD and depression in New York City residents five to eight weeks following the terrorist attacks was substantial, that Hispanic ethnicity and prior exposure to stress were associated with both PTSD and depression, and that losses resulting from the attacks were associated with depression.

there was a substantial burden in Manhattan of acute PTSD and acute depression in the months after the attacks, and that experiences involving exposure to the events and losses as a direct result of the events predicted the development of these symptoms.

7.5% of adults in Manhattan reported symptoms consistent with PTSD, 9.7% reported symptoms consistent with depression, and predictors of PTSD were Hispanic ethnicity, prior stressors, panic attacks, residence south of the World Trade Center, and losses, while predictors of depression were Hispanic, prior stressors and panic attacks, social support, loss of a relative or friend during the events, and loss of income or job.
